verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, upon Shoshannim, a testimony, of Asaph, a psalm.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to be sung to the tune called "Lilies" — a testimony, from Asaph's guild, a psalm.
verses.directors_commentary: This is not part of the prayer; it is the program note, and the Hebrew counts it as a verse of its own, which is why the KJV numbering runs one behind from here on (KJV 80:1 is Hebrew verse 2). Treat it as the cue card handed to the singers. Nobody knows for certain what "upon Shoshannim" means. It may name a melody ("Lilies"), an instrument, or a lily-shaped object; Metzudat Zion says an instrument made in the form of a lily, while Rashi, reading Song 2:2, takes the lily as Israel herself. "Eduth" is likewise disputed: Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion link it to 'adi, "ornament" (2 Kings 11:12), Meiri also offers "statute", and the Targum makes it a "testimony" of the Torah. The KJV does the honest thing and leaves "Shoshannim–Eduth" untranslated as one word, which hides that the Hebrew has two. The cantor's label matters for the performance only in one way: this is liturgy. It belongs to a guild, the sons of Asaph, who sang in the temple, and it was composed for many voices, as the refrain will show.

philological_notes.note: Literally "to the one who excels/leads"; a title given to the music director of the temple choir. 'Choirmaster' is a convention, not a certainty. Radak says these psalm headings concern matters of performance that were no longer known in his day.
'Testimony'; the same word names the tablets in the ark. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion connect it to 'adi, "adornment" (2 Kings 11:12), Meiri also to "statute"; the Targum has "testimony of the Torah".

verses.translation_literal: Shepherd of Israel, give ear! Leader, like the flock, of Joseph! Sitter of the cherubim, shine forth!
verses.translation_dramatic: Shepherd of Israel, hear us! You who lead Joseph the way a shepherd leads his flock — you who sit enthroned above the cherubim — shine out!
verses.directors_commentary: The cry opens with three titles, each pressed against the next like a hand on a door. A shepherd is the stock image for a king in the ancient Near East, so the singers are calling their God by a royal name and a humble one together. Notice who is the flock: "Joseph", not Israel. By this psalm's time "Joseph" can stand for the northern tribes (Ephraim and Manasseh are his sons) and, as Rashi, Radak and Meiri all say, for all Israel; Rashi ties it to Joseph's feeding of his family in the famine. The third title is the throne image: the ark of the covenant had a golden lid with two winged cherubim, and God was said to meet Israel "from between" them (Exod 25:22, which Rashi cites). The KJV's "dwellest between the cherubims" is both archaic and an invented plural: the Hebrew has the plain participle "sitting" and the Hebrew plural is already -im. The last word, hofi'ah, is a lamp imperative: "shine forth", the verb of Sinai (Deut 33:2, which Metzudat Zion cites). Play it as a command spoken in desperation, not as a polite request. The imperatives in the first verse (hear, shine) carry the whole tone of the psalm.

philological_notes.note: "Shepherd", also "ruler". Used by Jacob in Gen 48:15 and 49:24, as Ibn Ezra notes, where God is the shepherd of Joseph; this is almost certainly the echo the psalmist wants.
Literally "the one sitting (on) the cherubim"; the participle gives the throne image. Rashi connects it to the meeting-place above the ark (Exod 25:22).
"Shine forth", "appear radiantly". The same verb is used for God's appearance at Sinai (Deut 33:2). Rashi glosses it as "show your might".

verses.translation_literal: Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh, rouse [obj] your might, and come for salvation for us.
verses.translation_dramatic: Before Ephraim, before Benjamin, before Manasseh — stand where they can see you and wake your strength. Wake it! Come. Come for our rescue.
verses.directors_commentary:
The three names are not a random list. Ephraim and Manasseh are Joseph's sons, and Benjamin is Rachel's second child; these are the Rachel tribes, who marched together behind the ark in the wilderness camp (Num 2), and the verse before has just named Joseph. Ephraim comes first because it led the northern kingdom, as Ibn Ezra notes: he names Ephraim first as Jacob did, and because it was the standard-bearer. Play the line as a cry from the north, spoken by people who know the shepherd's throne is in the south.

'Rouse your might' uses the verb of waking a sleeper: the singer treats the divine warrior as asleep, an image the Psalms use boldly (Ps 44:24; 78:65) and the surrounding gods' myths of sleeping and waking deities would have made vivid. Then comes the word that splits the commentators. The KJV 'and come and save us' takes ולכה as a verb of motion plus a noun, 'for our salvation', but smooths over two things: 'and come' is spoken in a form that the masoretic tradition reads as 'yours' (לך), as Rashi, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion hold: 'it is for you, it falls to you to save', whether the people are worthy or not. Ibn Ezra reports that the masoretes say this and rejects it ('this explanation is not right in my eyes'). Radak and Meiri read the plain verb, 'go before us to save us' (Meiri adds: 'swiftly'), and Meiri keeps the 'yours' reading as another option. The literal layer follows the verb. A director can use both: 'come!' with the weight of 'this is yours to do'.

The verse ends on 'for us': after the tribes and the might, the singers finally name themselves as the ones in need.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of the verb 'to wake, rouse', here used for the divine might as if it had been sleeping. The same verb is used for waking a sleeper or stirring a warrior.

Either the imperative 'and go/come' (Radak, Meiri) or, by the masorah, 'and yours' (= ולך, 'it rests on you'), as Rashi, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion read it; Ibn Ezra reports the masoretic reading and rejects it. Rashi cites Gen 27:37, 2 Sam 18:22 and Isa 3:6 for the form.

verses.translation_literal: God, bring us back, and make your face shine, and let us be saved.
verses.translation_dramatic: God — bring us back. Turn your face toward us and let it shine, and let us be saved.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the first of three refrains (vv. 4, 8, 20), each longer than the last. Here it is bare: 'Elohim' alone, with no 'hosts' and no 'YHWH'. The singers begin with the most general name and climb as the psalm goes on.

'Bring us back' is the causative of the verb 'to turn, return', and the object is the people, not a place. Ibn Ezra reads 'help us to turn to you'; Radak, 'direct our hearts to you'; Metzudat David, 'to you'. Meiri, Malbim and the Targum read it as return from exile. The Hebrew does not say which; do not decide for the actors, let the line carry both. The KJV 'turn us again' keeps the ambiguity but archaizes it.

'Make your face shine' is the language of the priestly blessing (Num 6:25), where the shining face is favor; Radak spells it out: in anger God hides his face, in favor he lets it shine. The KJV renders the last verb 'and we shall be saved', a promise. The Hebrew is a cohortative, 'and let us be saved', still part of the prayer: shine, and let us be saved. The plea ends on the thing it is asking for, not on a guarantee.

philological_notes.note: Hifil imperative of 'to return', 'make us return' or 'bring us back'. Whether it means repentance or restoration from exile is not settled by the grammar; Ibn Ezra and Radak read inner return, Meiri, Malbim and the Targum exile.
'And make your face shine': an idiom for favor, as in the priestly blessing. Radak: in a time of anger he hides his face, in a time of favor he shines it.
Nifal cohortative, 'and let us be saved': a wish, not the KJV promise 'we shall be saved'.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, God of hosts, until when have you smoked at the prayer of your people?
verses.translation_dramatic: LORD, God of armies — how long? How long will you burn, and the smoke of it rise over the prayer your people send up?
verses.directors_commentary:
The KJV 'how long wilt thou be angry against the prayer of thy people' turns a picture into an abstraction and also changes the tense. The Hebrew verb is 'ashanta, 'you have smoked', from 'ashan, smoke: God is a fire whose smoke has not stopped rising. Ancient listeners knew the image: 'smoke went up from his nostrils' (Ps 18:9), and Mount Sinai was 'all smoke' when God came down in fire (Exod 19:18), both of which Ibn Ezra cites. Metzudat Zion links it to Ps 74:1, 'why does your anger smoke against the flock of your pasture?'. Play it as heat and breath: an angry deity breathing smoke at the very people who are praying.

The commentators split on what the smoke does. Radak, Metzudat David and Meiri's second reading take it as God's anger smoking 'at' or 'against' the prayer, so that the prayer never calms him. Ibn Ezra and Meiri's first reading turn it around: the prayer itself has become like smoke, smoke rising and not being received (Meiri: incense, Ps 141:2, is pleasant; smoke is not). The preposition ב fits either 'at' or 'during'. The Targum smooths it to 'you have not accepted the prayer of your people'. Meiri also records a medical-physiological theory that anger is the boiling of the heart's blood, and the heat comes out as smoke through the nose; he compares 'a fire is kindled in my anger' (Jer 15:14).

The divine title is a stack: YHWH, Elohim, Tzevaot. The first is the personal name, the last 'hosts' (armies, or the heavenly host). Radak and Meiri read the middle as a construct with a missing word, 'God, God of hosts'; Ibn Ezra reads it as two titles together. The refrain has now grown by one name from verse 4. 'Until when' is the classic cry of lament: not a request for information but a demand that the anger have an end.

philological_notes.note: Qal perfect of a verb from the noun 'smoke': 'you have smoked'. Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion gloss it as 'be angry', Metzudat Zion linking it to Ps 74:1 ('your anger smokes'); Ibn Ezra reads it as the prayer being like smoke (Exod 19:18, Ps 18:9).

'At the prayer of your people': the preposition can be 'at', 'against' or 'during'. Meiri gives two readings, the prayer as smoke instead of incense (Ps 141:2) or God's anger smoking against the prayer (Jer 15:14).

verses.translation_literal: You have fed them bread of tear, and made them drink tears by the third-measure.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have fed them on bread made of weeping, and poured them tears to drink — measure upon heavy measure.
verses.directors_commentary: Two meals, both of grief. "Bread of a tear" is a Hebrew construct chain: the bread is made of tears or eaten with them, and the singular "tear" (dim'ah) collects every tear into one substance. Then the drink: "tears by the shalish". A shalish is a measure, literally a "third", and the commentators do not agree on what of: Isa 40:12 uses it for the dust of the earth, which Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Metzudat Zion take as a large measure; the rabbis later read it as a third of an ephah, a third exile, or the three tears of Esau (Rashi). Tradition even worked out that Babylon's seventy years are a third of Egypt's 210. What stays certain is the effect: water is something a person drinks in measures, and the measure is large. The KJV's "great measure" is the safest rendering, YLT's "a third time" is a minority reading. Note the grammar: both verbs are causatives, "you have made them eat, you have made them drink", so the one who is addressed is the cause of the grief. This is what makes the psalm a protest.

philological_notes.note: "Bread of tears". Ibn Ezra and Meiri read an omitted bet: "bread with tears"; Metzudat David "in place of bread, tears". Meiri and Radak apply it to continuous suffering.

A measure whose size is unknown; elsewhere only Isa 40:12 ("a shalish of dust"). Metzudat Zion and Meiri call it a large measure. Rashi lists other interpretations, including Menachem's "a drinking vessel".

token_glosses.gloss: and you have made them drink

verses.translation_literal: You set us [as] a strife to our neighbors, and our enemies mock among themselves.
verses.translation_dramatic: You make us a quarrel for our neighbors to fight over, and our enemies laugh behind their hands.
verses.directors_commentary: From the private grief to the public humiliation. A madon is a quarrel, a contention. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David take it as "people who litigate": Israel is the case on every neighbor's docket, or the prize they argue over. Meiri: a source of constant fighting. The final "yil'agu lamo" is a puzzle: lamo is an archaic form of "to them", and the KJV's "among themselves" takes it as the enemies talking to each other. Radak adds a more daring reading, that they mock "him", God himself, by saying he cannot save; Ibn Ezra treats the suffix as a reverent circumlocution for God. The Hebrew allows either. Play it with the laughter overheard rather than shouted. The verb "you make us" again puts the responsibility on God; this continues the complaint from the previous verse. For the audience, the shame is the point: in ancient Near Eastern culture a defeated people was mocked as having a god who failed.

philological_notes.note: "Strife, contention", related to din, "judgment, legal dispute". Metzudat David: litigants and quarrelers; Meiri: constant fighting.
Archaic "to them". Metzudat Zion: "to themselves", i.e. at them; Radak also reads "at God". Ibn Ezra reads the suffix as a reverent reference to God.

verses.translation_literal: God of hosts, bring us back, and make your face shine, and let us be saved.
verses.translation_dramatic: God of armies — bring us back. Let your face shine upon us, and let us be saved.
verses.directors_commentary:
The second refrain adds a word: 'hosts'. Radak says one prays the same words three times to strengthen the plea, but with a small change each time. The change here is the title, from 'God' to 'God of hosts', the divine warrior with the armies of heaven. The sentence itself is verse 4, word for word, and the actors should hear it as a repeat, not a new thought.

The KJV keeps the refrain visible ('Turn us again, O God of hosts, and cause thy face to shine'), but 'turn us again' is archaic and flattens 'bring us back', and the final verb is again a cohortative, 'and let us be saved', not the KJV's promise.

Stage direction: between verses 4 and 8 the singers have said that God has fed them tears and made them a joke to their neighbors (vv. 5-7). So the same words sound different the second time, harder and more tired.

philological_notes.note: 'God of hosts', with 'YHWH' omitted; the same title grows to 'YHWH Elohim Tzevaot' in v. 20. Radak reads each repetition as the same plea with a small change.

verses.translation_literal: A vine from Egypt you uprooted; you drove out nations and planted it.
verses.translation_dramatic: Out of Egypt you lifted a vine. You drove the nations from the ground, and you planted it there.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the psalm turns from complaint to memory, and the image changes from shepherd to gardener. A vine is the standard metaphor for Israel (Isa 5:7, which Meiri cites), and the story is the Exodus and the conquest told in the language of farming. Taking a vine out of Egypt is more violent than the KJV's "brought": the verb nasa' is the word for pulling up tent pegs, which is why Rashi quotes Job 19:10, "He uprooted my hope like a tree", and why Ibn Ezra links it to the wilderness march. The verbs are "you uprooted" and "you drove out" in the imperfect, which Radak says stands for the past. The KJV's "thou hast cast out the heathen" is both the wrong register, "heathen" is a Christian word, and wrong for goyim, which simply means "nations". The chapter's image will not be left behind: the vine will be broken in verse 13, and the whole psalm lives in the contrast. Let this verse be told with pride, so the fall hurts.

philological_notes.note: "Vine"; here Israel as God's vineyard. Meiri cites Isa 5:7, "the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel".
Causative of nasa', "to pull up (tent pegs), set out". Said of a vine it means "uproot". Rashi cites Job 19:10 and Chullin 92a.

verses.translation_literal: You cleared before it, and it rooted its roots, and it filled [the] land.
verses.translation_dramatic: You cleared the ground before it. It sank its roots deep, and it filled the land.
verses.directors_commentary: The gardener's work: first clearing, then rooting, then growth. The Hebrew carries a pun the KJV's "preparedst room" loses: pinita lefaneha, "you cleared before its face", with the same word, pnh, as the "face" that God is asked to make shine. The one who cleared its face is asked to show his own face now. The vine's growth is told with root words stacked on each other: vatashresh shorasheiha, "it rooted its roots", a figura etymologica that the KJV's "take deep root" flattens. In the garden metaphor the cleared ground is the nations' land; Ibn Ezra reads it as clearing stones from a field, and he says the stones are the wicked. Radak gives the plain sense: no one stood before them. The sentence then ends, short, with "filled the land": make the audience wait on the pause.

philological_notes.note: "You cleared", "made empty"; the root pnh also gives panim, "face", the same root as the key word of the refrain. Metzudat Zion: removal and emptying of a place.
Verb and noun from the same root: "it rooted its roots". Rashi glosses it "you caused it to root its roots"; Ibn Ezra and Radak discuss the conjugation.

verses.translation_literal: Covered were mountains [with] its shade, and its branches [were] cedars of God.
verses.translation_dramatic: The mountains lay under its shade, covered by it as a cloak covers a sleeper; and its branches reached out like the cedars of God, tall and unbowed.
verses.directors_commentary:
The vine has filled the land, and now it climbs the mountains. The image is large: shade the size of a mountain range, branches the size of cedars. The Hebrew has no 'like' before 'cedars', so the KJV 'like the goodly cedars' and the ASV 'like cedars of God' insert a simile. In the Hebrew, the branches simply are 'cedars of God', and the vine is stretched beyond what vines do.

The grammar of the first half is worth noticing. 'Were covered' is a passive (Pual), and the mountains are its subject; 'its shade' is then the thing they are covered with, an accusative of material, like 'one covers the naked with a garment', Ibn Ezra's second explanation. His first, and Radak's, supply a missing 'with': 'were covered with its shade'. The sense is the same and neither is wrong, but the KJV 'the hills were covered with the shadow of it' hides that the Hebrew puts the mountains first and the shade second, so the mountains are the ones acted on, and the shade is the cloth. Play it so that the audience sees the mountains pulled under a blanket.

'Cedars of God' ('arzei-'el) is the open question. Rashi reads 'strong cedars', that is, mighty kings; Radak, cedars so tall that one 'attaches God' to anything one wishes to enlarge; Metzudat Zion, 'el as strength, as in Ezek 31:11. The KJV 'goodly' turns the phrase into a soft compliment. Here the Hebrew word is the divine name itself, a superlative: cedars of the highest kind, God's own trees. For a listener, the cedars of Lebanon were the tallest trees anyone had ever seen, and they stood for royal power. The Targum goes further and reads the mountains as the mountains of Jerusalem, the shade as the Temple.

philological_notes.note: Pual 'were covered': mountains are the subject, 'its shade' an accusative of the covering material (Ibn Ezra's second option, 'like covering the naked with a garment'). Ibn Ezra's first option and Radak supply a missing bet, 'with its shade'.

'Cedars of God': a superlative, 'mighty cedars' (Rashi, who adds 'mighty kings'), 'very tall cedars' (Radak: one attaches 'el to anything one wants to magnify), 'el as strength (Metzudat Zion, citing Ezek 31:11).

verses.translation_literal: It sent out its shoots to the sea, and to the river its suckers.
verses.translation_dramatic: Its shoots reached out to the sea; its young tendrils, to the River.
verses.directors_commentary: The vine's borders are the promised borders. "The sea" is the Mediterranean, the western edge of the land (Num 34:6, which Rashi cites); "the river" is the Euphrates, the traditional ideal frontier (Josh 1:4, Rashi). Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri read the pair as length and breadth: from the Mediterranean (or the Philistines' sea) to the Euphrates. In the Hebrew the sentence is symmetric and tight: "to the sea"... "to the river"; the KJV's "boughs/branches" blurs two distinct words. The first, qetsir, normally means "harvest", so STEPBible's "branch" needs a defense: Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as a branch, comparing Job 14:9, "it makes a qatsir like a plant". The second, yonqot, are literally "nursing ones", the tender young shoots that suck sap from the main stem. The picture is of mother branches and nursing shoots. The cadence of this verse is the high point of the psalm: after it comes the break, in verse 13, "why have you broken down its walls?".

philological_notes.note: Usually "harvest"; here "branches", as in Job 14:9 ("he makes branches like a young plant"). Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as boughs.
Literally "its nursing ones", the tender young shoots. Radak: the soft branches of a year's growth; Metzudat Zion compares Isa 53:2.
"The River", meaning the Euphrates, the eastern limit of the promised land. Rashi cites Josh 1:4; Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as the breadth of the land.

verses.translation_literal: Why have you breached its walls, and they have plucked it, all passers-by of [the] road?
verses.translation_dramatic: Why? Why did you pull down the walls you raised, and leave the vine standing open to the road, so that every stranger who hurries past reaches out a hand and strips it?
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hinge of the psalm: the vine of the previous verses, so lavish that its shade covered mountains and its tendrils reached the sea and the River, is suddenly naked to the road. Play the question not as a charge but as bewilderment; the speakers cannot understand how the gardener could be the one who tore down the wall. In a Judean vineyard the גָּדֵר was a drystone wall, not a bush: farmers piled fieldstones into a low boundary against goats, jackals and thieves, and a breach in it meant the whole crop could be lost within a season. The KJV's 'hedges' is the soft, English-countryside picture; the Hebrew is hard stone, and it is YOU who have pulled it down (the verb פָּרַץ is the one for breaching a city wall). Isaiah 5:5 has the same image in the mouth of God himself, 'I will breach its wall and it will be trampled', which is what the psalmist now says has happened. The second half names who profits: not an army but 'all passers-by of the road', ordinary travellers with a free hand for ripe grapes. The verb אָרָה, 'to pluck', is the gentle harvester's word, as in Song 5:1 ('I have plucked my myrrh'), and that mildness is the cruelty: the vine is not ravaged by a conquest but picked over by whoever happens to pass. The KJV 'do pluck her' makes the vine feminine, which the Hebrew pronoun does, but 'her' in modern ears drifts to the vine as a person; keep it 'it' if you want the metaphor to stay a garden for now.

philological_notes.note: 'Its walls': a stone fence around a field or vineyard. KJV 'hedges' and BBE 'walls' differ; the root means to wall in, and the noun is used of sheepfolds and vineyard boundaries alike. Metzudat Zion glosses the word with כתליה, 'its walls'.
'And they have plucked it': to gather or pluck fruit, with the same verb in Song 5:1. Rashi ties it to a Mishnaic phrase for a basket of gathered produce.

verses.translation_literal: It gnaws it, a boar from [the] forest, and the creatures that stir in [the] field graze on it.
verses.translation_dramatic: From the forest the boar comes, and it gnaws the vine to the root; the small things that crawl and stir out in the open fields come after and graze it bare.
verses.directors_commentary: The picture darkens: after the passers-by, the animals. The boar, חֲזִיר, is the worst thing a vineyard can meet; it roots, tramples and tears the vine from the ground in one night, which is why Israelite law counts it unclean and why the prophets use it as a byword for filth. The KJV 'wild beast of the field' is a guess at the rare word זִיז; its root means 'to move', and Rashi explains the word as 'all things that creep or stir in the field', so it is the lesser, restless creatures coming after the great one. The verb יְכַרְסְמֶנָּה is used nowhere else in the Bible and has a rasping, chewing sound; the voice should do what the consonants do. A famous scribal detail hangs over the verse: the letter ayin in מִיָּעַר is written raised above the line, and the tradition (Rashi, Radak, Meiri) notes it and plays on 'forest' (יער) against 'the river' (יאור), the Nile, whose creatures cannot leave the water. Whether or not an actor can speak a raised letter, the reading is that the oppressor has left the river and is now a forest animal, free to roam. The KJV's 'waste' and 'devour' are fair, but 'wood' is archaic for a forest. Later readers took the boar and the creatures as the nations, and Malbim as Nebuchadnezzar and his officers; the text itself names only animals.

philological_notes.note: 'It gnaws it': a rare four-letter verb, found only here. Ibn Ezra takes it as a quadriliteral like ירמסנה; the Mishnah has the same verb for ants gnawing a field, which Rashi cites.

'The creatures that stir in the field': זִיז from a root of moving; Rashi: 'everything that creeps in the field, from the verb to move from its place'. שָׂדַי is a poetic form of שָׂדֶה, as Ibn Ezra notes with a parallel from Psalm 96.

verses.translation_literal: God of hosts, return, please; look from heaven, and see, and attend to this vine.
verses.translation_dramatic: God of hosts, come back. Look down from heaven, we beg you, look and see, and tend this vine.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm turns from complaint to plea, and the grammar does it with a rush of imperatives: return, look, see, attend. Each is short and urgent; speak them as one breath that gets quieter, not louder. The KJV 'Return, we beseech thee' is faithful, but the Hebrew נָא is only a soft please, and 'look down from heaven' adds a direction the verb הַבֵּט does not need, although the phrase 'from heaven' is there. The first word is also a little shock: they ask God to RETURN, as though he had left the house. The same root שׁוּב is the refrain's 'restore us' (verses 4, 8, 20), so this plea is the refrain unfolded. The last verb פְּקֹד is the one for a visit that changes things: God musters a census, visits an unfulfilled promise, or inspects a vineyard for the damage. 'Visit', as in the KJV, is now a social call; it means 'attend to, take charge of'. The demonstrative זֹאת, 'this', is feminine, matching גֶּפֶן, and points at something the speakers can see: the vine in front of them, still the same vine God once carried out of Egypt (Ibn Ezra reads 'this' as the very vine God uprooted from Egypt). Note that in the KJV the numbering is one lower, so this is 80:14 there.

philological_notes.note: 'And attend to': to visit with attention, whether for blessing or for judgment; here for care. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'attention, oversight'.
'God of hosts': Radak notes that the construct form of 'hosts' is not an adjective of God but a genitive, 'God of the hosts of heaven', and that it is the same title as 'YHWH, God of hosts'.

verses.translation_literal: And the stand which your right hand planted, and on [the] son you made strong for yourself.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look at the root your own right hand set in the earth, at the shoot you strengthened to be yours.
verses.directors_commentary: This verse has no verb of its own: it hangs on 'attend to' from the verse before, so the sentence should not be allowed to end at the pause. Two things are given to God's care, and both are described by what he did: he planted, he made strong. The first word, וְכַנָּה, appears nowhere else, and translators have had to guess. Rashi derives it from the base or stand of something, as in Genesis 40:13 where Pharaoh will restore the cupbearer 'to your place' (כַּנֶּךָ); Radak records two other ideas, 'a planting' and a variant of 'garden'. The KJV decided on 'vineyard', which smooths the oddity into a familiar word; YLT's 'root' and ASV's 'stock' are closer to the sense of a base. The second half says 'on the son', where בֵּן means a shoot of a vine just as in Genesis 49:22, 'Joseph is a fruitful bough' (בֵּן פֹּרָת). The KJV hides the pun by rendering it 'branch' while the same word reappears in verse 18 as 'son of man', and the audience should hear the connection: the shoot and the human son are the same word. 'Right hand' here is the hand of favour and power, the hand that carried Israel out. For the later reading, Ibn Ezra takes the stock as Israel; the Targum, in the packet, makes the son 'the king, the Messiah'.

philological_notes.note: 'And the stand': found only here. Rashi: 'what is fixed and settled', citing Gen 40:13; Radak and Meiri also give 'planting' and a possible variant of גנה, 'garden', since the consonants כ and ג are close; the sense is disputed.
'Son', here used for a shoot or branch of the vine; Ibn Ezra cites 'a fruitful bough' (בֵּן פֹּרָת) and the word returns as 'son of man' in verse 18.

verses.translation_literal: Burned with fire, cut down; from the rebuke of your face they perish.
verses.translation_dramatic: Burned, it is burned with fire; hacked down, it lies cut. And the people go under, one after another, before the rebuke of your face.
verses.directors_commentary:
The vine of the previous verses is now a ruin, and the actors should play it as one. The two feminine participles, 'burned' and 'cut down', still describe the vine; the verb that closes the verse turns plural, 'they perish', and the picture slides from plant to people without a seam. Do not smooth that seam. The psalmist wants the audience to hear that what happened to the vine is happening to them.

The verse names the cause with a single phrase, 'the rebuke of your face'. Earlier the psalm spoke of what God did (fed them tears, made them a strife, breached the walls); here the destruction is traced to God's own face. That is the exact reverse of the refrain, 'make your face shine, that we may be saved' (80:4, 8, 20). The same face that can save by shining destroys by rebuking, so the prayer for light and this verse are two sides of one coin. Ibn Ezra says as much: this is 'the opposite of 'and make your face shine''. The KJV renders the word as 'countenance', an archaizing, polite word that drains the body from it; the Hebrew is simply 'face', the one the refrain keeps asking to see. It also supplies 'it is' twice, which is fair English but hides that the Hebrew simply piles two participles: 'burned... cut down'.

For the first audience, burning and cutting are what happens to a vine nobody tends: prunings and brush were burned in the field, and an invading army cut vines for fuel and siege works. Rashi ties 'cut down' (kesuchah) to the verb of pruning in Leviticus 25:4, and Meiri notes the rabbinic point that a vine that is pruned, not uprooted, can grow again from the trunk. That hope is the quiet undertone of the verse.

philological_notes.note: 'Cut down'. A rare word. The Targum renders the same verb at Leviticus 25:4 as 'do not cut', and Rashi and Metzudat Zion link it to the pruning of the vine and to 'cut-down thorns' in Isaiah 33:12. Meiri adds that a pruned vine can sprout again from its trunk, so the word may carry a thread of hope.

'From the rebuke of your face'. The destruction is traced to God's face itself, the reverse of the refrain's 'make your face shine'. Ibn Ezra reads it explicitly as the opposite of 'and make your face shine'; Radak glosses it as God hiding his face and rebuking them.

verses.translation_literal: May your hand be on the man of your right hand, on the son of humankind you made strong for yourself.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let your hand rest on him, the man at your right hand, the one you took and made strong to be your own, a son of Adam, a mortal, and yours.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the ruin, the prayer turns on a single wish: 'may your hand be on...'. Whose hand, and for what? Ibn Ezra gives a rule: when 'hand of the LORD' is followed by the preposition ב ('in, against'), it is for harm ('the hand of the LORD was against them'); when there is no ב, it is for help ('may your hand be to help me'). Here the preposition is 'al, 'on', with no ב, so on his rule the wish is for help: let your hand cover and steady him. Not every old reader hears it so. Rashi and Malbim both read a blow: Rashi says 'bring your blows back on Esau', the man from whom your right hand is to exact payment; Malbim sees the enemy, the one who came with the strength of God's own right hand to lay countries waste, and asks that the blow of God's hand fall on the man God's right hand had strengthened. The Hebrew allows both. The actors must choose, and the choice changes the scene: a hand that shields, or a hand that strikes.

'The man of your right hand' is the one at God's strong side, the place of honor and protection. Whom does it mean? Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David read the people, Israel, bought 'with your right hand and your great arm' (Radak), the man you saved by your right hand (Metzudat David). Ibn Ezra offers the vine's shoot or a figure he calls the messiah of Ephraim; Rashi and Malbim, as above, read an enemy. The second line, 'son of humankind', only repeats the first: 'a doubling' (Radak). Meiri notes a neat link back to the vine: the earlier verse had a 'son' (ben) in the sense of a branch, and now the branch has become a ben adam.

The KJV, 'the son of man', is a literal rendering and is not wrong, but today's reader hears a title. In Hebrew, ben adam is just a mortal, a human being, with a note of frailty; later readers heard a title in the phrase, and it helps to play it low here: a frail person, held up by God's strength. The last word, 'for yourself' (lakh), says that the strength was given for God's purposes; the dependence runs in one direction.

philological_notes.note: Ibn Ezra's rule: 'hand' followed by ב is for harm, without it for help. Here it is 'al, with no ב, so 'may your hand be on' is on his rule a plea for help. Rashi ('bring your blows back on Esau') and Malbim ('the blow of your hand') take it as a blow; the Hebrew does not exclude that.

'The man of your right hand'. The one at God's right side, the strong side. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David read it as Israel, bought 'with your right hand and your great arm' (Radak). Rashi reads Esau, the man from whom the right hand is to exact payment; Malbim reads the enemy who came with the strength of God's right hand.
'Son of humankind', that is, a mortal. The Hebrew phrase itself is generic. Radak calls the line a doubling of the first half; Meiri ties it to the 'son' as a branch of the vine, now a person.

'You made strong for yourself'. A piel of the root for strength. 'For yourself' states that the strength is God's gift for God's own purposes. Radak reads it as 'one who was with you and to whom you were God'; Rashi ties it to Esau's dwelling 'of the fat of the earth' (Genesis 27:39).

verses.translation_literal: And we will not turn back from you; you will give us life, and in your name we will call.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then we will never turn away from you. Give us life, and we will call on your name.
verses.directors_commentary: A vow folded into the plea. 'We will not turn back from you' uses the verb of a retreating army and of apostasy, and it is the exact opposite of what the speakers ask God to do in verse 15. They want him to come back, and they promise not to leave. The KJV's 'So will not we go back' adds a 'so' that the Hebrew does not have, which makes the vow a consequence; the Hebrew simply sets 'we will not turn back' next to 'give us life', and the listener decides the order. The verb תְּחַיֵּנוּ, literally 'you will make us live', is the language of resurrection from near death; Rashi and Radak hear it as life out of exile, which Radak calls 'the death of exile'. The KJV 'quicken' is an archaism for 'make alive'. The last clause, 'in your name we will call', is the ordinary Hebrew idiom for calling on God in prayer and worship; it is not 'we are called by your name', although that sense also hovers, and Radak adds 'and you are our redeemer'. The singular-to-plural shift in the speakers (the nation as one man in verse 18, now 'we') is natural biblical style, as Meiri notes.

philological_notes.note: 'We will turn back': to draw back or retreat, here from loyalty. Metzudat Zion cites a verse with the same verb for turning from God.
'You will give us life': the intensive stem, 'bring to life, revive'. Radak: 'from the death of exile'.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, God of hosts, bring us back; make your face shine, and let us be saved.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD, God of hosts, bring us home. Let your face shine on us, and we will be saved.
verses.directors_commentary: The refrain for the third time, now at its fullest. It first appeared as 'God, restore us' (verse 4), then 'God of hosts' (verse 8), and now 'YHWH, God of hosts', which is the whole name. Rashi and Meiri read the growing title as the growing weight of the exile and the plea: the longer the trouble, the longer the address. The KJV 'Turn us again' is archaic; the verb הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ is 'bring us back', the same root as 'return' in verse 15, so that the people ask God to return and to return them, and the same word covers both: 'turn' as repentance and 'turn' as bringing home. 'Cause thy face to shine' is literal and should stay as it is: the face that scowled in verse 17 is now asked to light up, as in the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:25). The final verb is a cohortative passive: 'and let us be saved', or 'so that we may be saved'; the salvation is not a separate request but the result of the face turned the right way. The KJV 'we shall be saved' reads it as a promise, while the Hebrew mood is a wish. Radak sets the shining face against the earlier rebuking face (verse 17). End quietly: this is the line the audience carries out of the room.

philological_notes.note: 'Bring us back, restore us': the causative of 'turn' and the psalm's refrain verb (verses 4, 8, 20). KJV 'turn us again' hides that it is God who is asked to turn people.
'Make your face shine': the language of favour. Radak reads it as the answer to 'the rebuke of your face' in verse 17.
'And let us be saved': first person plural cohortative of the passive stem, a wish rather than a promise.
